Every layer we profiled had something odd about it. We wrote down 39 of them, each with a count and what we do about it.
Kinds of quirk
No stable identifier
on parcels, addresses and secondary plans. We mint our own.
Geometry problems:
stacked duplicate parcels, invalid shapes as served (205 of 271 rows in one regulated-areas layer), rows with no geometry at all.
Two maps that do not quite line up:
a consistent shift of about one metre between two parcel layers.
Fields that mean something else:
a field called "full street" that holds the street number; a layer titled "heavy truck traffic route" that holds all-vehicle counts.
Conventions:
blanks stored as a single space; yes and no stored as -1 and 0; dates stored as text; heights printed as 3.8000000000000003.
Stale or constant values:
a version field that is 0 on every row; metadata describing a plan two updates old.
Codes nobody has defined for us yet:
restriction and load codes on road layers. We show them marked "meaning not yet confirmed" and have asked the City.
Personal and business identifiers
in public layers: staff account names, company names, private rail spur names. These are screened at the point of publishing.
Why write them down

A quirk found once and fixed silently will be found again by the next person, or the next city. Each one has a handling rule, so the fix is the same every time the layer is pulled. The short field notes in this section tell some of them one at a time.
